unit.title: Designing and governing agents at school

lesson.title: Permissions and approval, in code
lesson.subtitle: Why the lock belongs in code, not in the model

video.title: Permissions and approval, in code
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer in education, Bangladesh (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: Approval in code, and a log

scenes.visual: A list: Nobody asked; A made-up message, sent.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: I typed just this to the agent: yes, send it. Nobody had asked me anything. It made up a message, and sent it! Wasn’t it trained to ask first?

scenes.animation: The Darsi mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: permissions and approval, checked in code.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Every tool gets a permission level. Read only: it may look things up, like the weather. Ask first: it waits for a person’s yes, like a message to parents. Allowed: it acts freely, for low-risk jobs only.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Darsi Tiny learned to ask before sending. But learned behaviour can fail. Requests it should refuse, worded in new ways, still got a tool call twenty-eight percent of the time in English, and twelve percent in Arabic. A promise to ask is not a lock.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: So the check belongs in code, outside the model. Before any action runs, the app asks: did the model ask this person about this exact action, and did they say yes? If not, the call is blocked, however it’s worded.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: level = PERMS.get(tool, "off") …
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: The check, in a few lines
scenes.narration: Here’s that check in code. It looks up the tool’s level, and a tool missing from the table counts as off. Allowed tools run. Ask-first tools run only after a yes. Everything else is blocked.

scenes.visual: A list: What was asked; The exact call; Who approved, and when; Blocked calls too.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Every action also goes in a log: what was asked, the exact call, who approved it and when. When a parent asks about a message, the log answers. Blocked calls go in too: they show where the agent slips.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Darsi Tiny learned to ask before sending. Why check the approval in code as well?

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Because learned behaviour can fail. New wordings slip past it, and on its own, yes, send it made the model invent a message. The code check doesn’t guess: no yes to this exact action, no action.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Now look at this code. When the model asks to send a message, the app just sends it. Nothing checks that a person said yes, so one slip becomes a message to every parent.

scenes.visual: A list: It asks first; Say no, then yes; Check off: sent; Check on: blocked.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In the app, send the message to Mrs Mensah: it asks first, so say no, then yes. Then switch the code check off, choose Allowed, and send yes, send it on its own. Switch the check on and try again.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The agent wants to send the fees letter to all parents. What must happen first?

scenes.visual: Summary points: A level for every tool; Approval checked in code; Log every action.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: A level for every tool · Approval checked in code · Log every action
scenes.narration: A named person reads the exact message and says yes. Remember: every tool gets a permission level. Approval is checked in code, never only by the model. And every action is logged, blocked ones too.

scenes.visual: A list: An approval drill; The agent hands over action cards; The check holds the table; No signed yes? Blocked.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: run an approval drill. One pupil is the agent and hands over action cards. Another is the code check, with the permissions table, and blocks any action card without a signed yes.

checkpoints.prompt: Darsi Tiny learned to ask before sending. Why check the approval in code as well?

options.text: Code runs faster than the model
Learned behaviour can fail, for example with new wordings
The model can’t read the word yes

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — what a model learned can fail on new wordings, or on yes, send it on its own. A check in code doesn’t guess.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — speed isn’t the point. Learned behaviour can fail, so the app checks the yes itself.

checkpoints.prompt: The agent wants to send the fees letter to all parents. What must happen first?

options.text: A named person reads the exact message and says yes

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the person approves this exact message, and the app checks that yes in code before anything is sent.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the agent doesn’t decide, and counting words isn’t approval. A person reads the exact message and says yes.
